title: Seeds and Germination
tagline: Bean seed and maize grain, monocot and dicot, hypogeal and epigeal germination, and the conditions a seed needs to begin growth.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A seed is the reproductive unit produced after fertilisation in flowering plants, and it is one of the most important structures in the plant life cycle because it allows a new plant to begin life in a protected, self-contained way. This chapter studies the structure of a bean seed and a maize grain, compares monocot and dicot seeds, describes the conditions needed for germination, and follows the two patterns of germination — epigeal and hypogeal — as the seedling emerges and begins to grow on its own.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: A seed contains an embryo, a food store and a protective coat, allowing a new plant to start from a dormant unit

facts.label: Two examples
facts.value: Bean seed as a dicot example and maize grain as a monocot example

facts.label: Germination patterns
facts.value: Epigeal, where cotyledons appear above ground, and hypogeal, where they stay below

learn.title: The seed as a unit of reproduction

blocks.text: A seed is the product of fertilisation and is made of three main parts: the embryo, which is the young plant; the food store, which supplies energy and materials for early growth; and the protective seed coat, which shields the embryo from damage, drying and infection. In a dry seed the embryo is usually dormant, meaning it is alive but not growing; when conditions become favourable it becomes active and germination begins. The seed is therefore both a means of dispersal and a way of surviving unfavourable seasons. Its structure reflects these tasks: protection, storage and a ready embryo.

items.meaning: Mature ovule containing an embryo, a food store and a protective coat.
The young plant inside the seed, made of the radicle, plumule and one or two cotyledons.
Seed leaf that may store food or help in transfer of food to the embryo.
Protective outer covering of the seed, also called testa in many seeds.
A state in which a living seed does not germinate even in favourable conditions until its needs are met.
The process by which a seed develops into a seedling, beginning with the emergence of the radicle.

items: A seed contains an embryo, a food store and a protective seed coat.
The embryo includes the radicle, the plumule and one or two cotyledons.
The food store may be in the cotyledons or in a special tissue called endosperm.
A dry seed may be dormant until the right conditions for germination are present.
Germination usually begins with the emergence of the radicle, the future root.
The seed coat protects the embryo from damage and drying.

items.text: A bean seed is large enough to see the seed coat, the two cotyledons and the embryo between them.
items.note: The bean seed is the standard dicot example in ICSE work because its parts are easy to recognise.

items.text: A maize grain has the embryo along one side and most of the grain filled with food tissue, not with free cotyledons as in the bean.
items.note: Maize shows how a monocot seed can be organised differently from a bean.

learn.title: Bean seed and maize grain compared

blocks.text: A bean seed is the most common dicot example used in ICSE Biology. The outer seed coat, or testa, is protective and may have a small scar, the hilum, where the seed was attached to the pod, and a tiny opening, the micropyle, through which water can enter. Inside are two large cotyledons that store food, and between them the embryo. The embryo has a radicle, a plumule and a small axis. When the seed is soaked, the seed coat softens and the cotyledons become visible. A maize grain is a monocot example. It has a tough outer covering and a large endosperm that stores food. The embryo lies on one side and includes the radicle, plumule and a single cotyledon, the scutellum, which helps transfer food from the endosperm to the growing embryo. So the main contrast is that the bean stores food in two large cotyledons, while maize stores it mainly in endosperm and has only one cotyledon.

items.meaning: The seed coat of a seed, forming the protective outer layer.
The scar on a seed where it was attached to the fruit or pod.
A tiny opening in the seed coat through which water can enter during germination.
Food storage tissue in many seeds, such as maize, that nourishes the embryo.
The single cotyledon of a monocot grain such as maize, involved in transferring food to the embryo.
The part of the embryo that develops into the root.
The part of the embryo that develops into the shoot and leaves.

items: A bean seed has a testa, two food-storing cotyledons and an embryo between them.
The hilum is the scar of attachment and the micropyle is the tiny opening for water entry.
A maize grain has a large endosperm and a single cotyledon called the scutellum.
In the bean the cotyledons are the main food store; in maize the endosperm is the main food store.
Both types have a radicle and a plumule in the embryo.
The two examples show the typical organisation of dicot and monocot seeds.

items.text: Soaking a bean seed makes the testa peel easily and reveals the two cotyledons and the embryo.
items.note: Soaking is a common first step in examining a seed in the laboratory.

items.text: A cut maize grain shows a large starchy portion and a small embryo on the side.
items.note: The contrast between the food mass and the embryo is easier to see in a grain than in a bean.

blocks.text: Germination does not begin in every seed at every moment. It usually requires water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Water is needed to soften the seed coat, allow the tissues to become active and help the food become available to the embryo. Oxygen is needed for respiration, because the growing embryo uses energy released from food. A suitable temperature is needed because the chemical reactions of growth are controlled by enzymes, and enzymes work only within a certain temperature range. Some seeds also need light or the breaking of dormancy before they will germinate, but water, oxygen and suitable temperature are the three basic conditions usually tested in ICSE work. If any one is missing, germination will be slow or will not occur at all.

items.meaning: Needed in germination to soften the seed coat and make stored food available to the embryo.
Needed for respiration so the embryo can release energy from food for growth.
A temperature range that allows the enzymes of germination to work.
The process by which the embryo releases energy from food, requiring oxygen.

items: The three main conditions for germination are water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Water softens the seed coat and helps stored food become available.
Oxygen is required for respiration, which releases energy for growth.
A suitable temperature is needed because enzymes control germination.
If any condition is missing, germination may fail or be very slow.
Some seeds have extra needs such as light or dormancy-breaking signals.

items.text: A seed kept in a vacuum or sealed dry container will not germinate because it cannot get oxygen or water.
items.note: This shows that all three conditions must be present together.

items.text: Seeds stored in a cool, dry place stay dormant because the conditions are not suitable for growth.
items.note: Storage uses the same principles as germination in reverse.

blocks.text: Once germination begins, the seedling grows in one of two main patterns. In epigeal germination the cotyledons are carried above the ground as the seedling emerges; the epicotyl grows and pulls the cotyledons upward, so the seed leaves appear above the soil. In hypogeal germination the cotyledons remain below the ground, and only the plumule emerges above the surface while the cotyledons stay in the soil. The difference is not which part grows, but how the seedling is positioned as it emerges. Beans, for example, show epigeal germination, while maize and many other monocots show hypogeal germination. The pattern matters because it affects how the seedling uses its food store and how vulnerable it is when it first breaks the soil surface.

items.meaning: Germination in which the cotyledons are pushed above the ground.
Germination in which the cotyledons remain below the ground.
The part of the axis above the cotyledons, which grows upward in epigeal germination.
The part of the axis below the cotyledons, which often curves and pushes upward in epigeal germination.
The young plant that develops from a germinating seed.

items: In epigeal germination the cotyledons appear above the ground.
In hypogeal germination the cotyledons stay below the ground.
In epigeal germination the hypocotyl or epicotyl movement brings the cotyledons up.
Beans are a common example of epigeal germination.
Maize is a common example of hypogeal germination.
The pattern affects how the food store is used and how the seedling emerges.

items.text: A bean seedling often has its two cotyledons exposed above the soil, usually with their stored food partly used up.
items.note: Epigeal germination makes the seed leaves visible above ground.

items.text: A maize seedling usually sends up only the shoot, while the single cotyledon and endosperm stay below ground.
items.note: Hypogeal germination keeps the main food store hidden in the soil.

keyPoints: A seed contains an embryo, a food store and a protective seed coat.
The embryo includes the radicle, plumule and one or two cotyledons.
The bean seed stores food in two cotyledons; the maize grain stores food mainly in endosperm and has one cotyledon (scutellum).
The three main conditions for germination are water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Water softens the seed coat and makes food available; oxygen is needed for respiration; a suitable temperature is needed for enzyme action.
Epigeal germination brings the cotyledons above ground; hypogeal germination keeps them below ground.
Bean shows epigeal germination; maize shows hypogeal germination.
examFocus: Draw and label the main parts of a bean seed: testa, cotyledons, embryo, radicle and plumule.
State the function of the testa, micropyle, cotyledons and endosperm.

State the three conditions for germination and the function of each.
Distinguish epigeal and hypogeal germination with one example of each.

assessment.title: Seeds and Germination: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the seed parts, conditions or germination types clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.prompt: Name the three main parts of a seed.
exercises.answer: The three main parts of a seed are the embryo, the food store and the protective seed coat.
exercises.explanation: Each part should be named: embryo, food store and seed coat.

exercises.prompt: What is the function of the micropyle in a seed?
exercises.answer: The micropyle is a tiny opening in the seed coat through which water enters during germination.
exercises.explanation: The micropyle's function is to allow water entry to begin germination.

exercises.prompt: Distinguish the food storage in a bean seed and a maize grain.
exercises.answer: In a bean seed the food is stored in the two large cotyledons. In a maize grain the food is stored mainly in the endosperm, and the single cotyledon, the scutellum, helps transfer food to the embryo.
exercises.explanation: The contrast should mention cotyledons for the bean and endosperm for maize.

exercises.prompt: State the three conditions needed for germination and the function of one of them.
exercises.answer: The three conditions are water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Water softens the seed coat and makes stored food available to the embryo.
exercises.explanation: The three conditions should be named, and one function should be stated clearly.

exercises.answer: In epigeal germination the cotyledons are carried above the ground, as in the bean; in hypogeal germination the cotyledons remain below the ground, as in maize. In epigeal germination the shoot and cotyledons appear above the soil, while in hypogeal germination only the plumule usually becomes visible above ground.
exercises.explanation: The distinction should include the position of the cotyledons and one example.

exercises.prompt: Why is oxygen needed for germination?
exercises.answer: Oxygen is needed for respiration, because the embryo uses energy released from food to grow during germination.
exercises.explanation: The reason for oxygen is that germination requires respiration and energy release.

questions.prompt: The protective outer coat of a seed is the:
questions.explanation: The testa is the protective outer seed coat.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing endosperm — that is a food store, not the protective coat.

questions.prompt: The part of a seed that develops into the root is the:
questions.explanation: The radicle develops into the root of the seedling.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing plumule — that develops into the shoot, not the root.

questions.prompt: The maize grain has mainly which kind of food store?
questions.explanation: Maize stores food mainly in the endosperm.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing two cotyledons — that is the bean pattern, not the maize pattern.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the three main conditions needed for germination?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is needed for respiration during germination, along with water and a suitable temperature.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing light — light is not one of the three basic conditions in the usual ICSE answer.

questions.prompt: A bean seed shows which pattern of germination?
questions.explanation: A bean seedling shows epigeal germination, with the cotyledons appearing above ground.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing hypogeal — that is the maize pattern.

questions.prompt: The single cotyledon of a maize grain is the:
questions.explanation: The scutellum is the single cotyledon of a maize grain and helps transfer food to the embryo.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing endosperm — that is the food store, not the cotyledon.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the part of the embryo that develops into the shoot is the ________.
questions.explanation: The plumule develops into the shoot and leaves.
questions.commonMistake: Answering radicle — that develops into the root.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks: germination usually begins with the emergence of the ________, and water softens the ________.
questions.explanation: Germination begins with the radicle emerging, and water softens the seed coat.
questions.commonMistake: Switching the two blanks — the radicle emerges first and the seed coat is softened by water.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a bean seed.
questions.answer: A bean seed has a tough outer seed coat, or testa, which protects the inner parts. It has a hilum, the scar where it was attached to the pod, and a micropyle, a tiny opening through which water enters. Inside are two large cotyledons that store food, with the embryo between them. The embryo has a radicle, which becomes the root, and a plumule, which becomes the shoot.
questions.explanation: A good answer names the testa, hilum, micropyle, cotyledons and embryo with radicle and plumule.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only the seed coat and cotyledons and forgetting the radicle and plumule.

questions.prompt: State the three conditions needed for germination and the function of water.
questions.answer: The three conditions needed for germination are water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Water softens the seed coat and allows the stored food to become available to the embryo.
questions.explanation: The three conditions should be named, and the function of water should be stated clearly.
questions.commonMistake: Naming one condition as 'soil' or 'fertiliser' instead of the correct three.

questions.prompt: Compare a bean seed and a maize grain with respect to structure and food storage.
questions.answer: A bean seed is a dicot example with a protective testa, a hilum and a micropyle, and two large cotyledons that store most of the food. The embryo lies between the cotyledons and has a radicle and a plumule. A maize grain is a monocot example with a tough outer covering and a large endosperm that stores most of the food. It has only one cotyledon, the scutellum, which helps transfer food from the endosperm to the embryo. The embryo lies along one side of the grain. So the main differences are that the bean stores food in its two cotyledons, while maize stores food in its endosperm and has one cotyledon.
questions.explanation: A strong comparison covers food store, number of cotyledons and embryo position for both.
questions.commonMistake: Only saying one is a dicot and the other a monocot without describing the food storage difference.

questions.prompt: A seed is kept in a dry, airtight container. Will it germinate? Give reasons.
questions.answer: It will not germinate. Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. A dry, airtight container supplies no water, so the seed coat cannot be softened and the stored food cannot become available. It also prevents oxygen from reaching the seed, so respiration cannot release the energy needed for growth. Even if the temperature is suitable, the lack of water and oxygen means germination will not begin.
questions.explanation: The answer must link the dry, airtight conditions to the missing germination requirements.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that it may germinate if the temperature is right — the other conditions are still missing.
